note: EE GCC 3.2 codegen handbook, machine-readable index. Every law carries source_anchor (mainline file:line) and/or binary_anchor (shipped cc1 symbol/address). tier T1 = source rule + factory-binary anchor + matching behaviour; T2 = source rule OR binary anchor, plus behaviour; T3 = behaviour evidence only. No game content: anchors are compiler-internal symbols, addresses, line numbers and constants.

toolchain.probe_flags: -O2 -G0 (the conditions most measurements in this handbook were taken under)

laws.title: Global allocation order is allocno_compare: (floor_log2(n_refs) * freq) / live_length * (10000 / REG_FREQ_MAX) * size

source_anchor.note: mainline gcc-3.2.3 definition line; EE binary resolves the same function to global.c:789 (delta +175). Cite the EE line, use mainline for semantics.

symptom: allocation order differs from expectation
two values with the same reference count allocate in an unexpected order
lever: cross a power of two in n_refs (floor_log2 step)
move a use into a hotter block (freq is linear)
shorten the live range (live_length divides)
laws.receipt: 75 functions / 1,079 allocnos / 1,004 adjacent pairs: exact order 33/75, mean Kendall tau 0.873, 26 inversions (2.6%) [R28 §3]; formula constants corrected in R33 §4.3
laws.falsifies: dds-decomp's floor_log2(refs) * refs * hard_reg_width shape (all four local controls failed)
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 -G0; not tested on 2.96

laws.title: allocno.size is measured in WORDS, and the dump prints it only when size != 1

source_anchor.note: PSEUDO_REGNO_SIZE(N) = (GET_MODE_SIZE + UNITS_PER_WORD - 1) / UNITS_PER_WORD; global.c:1937 is the print condition `size != 1` (EE binary: global.c:2265)

symptom: no (N) size suffix appears in the `;; N regs to allocate:` line
a model that feeds bytes into the formula mis-ranks mixed-mode functions
lever: read the suffix as words: absent == 1 word (SImode), 2 words for DImode / DFmode
laws.receipt: zero `(N)` occurrences across the whole local corpus, including DFmode allocnos that do reach global allocation; SImode -> 1 word, DImode/DFmode -> 2 words
laws.falsifies: the reading that allocno.size is a byte count (the R28 tool substituted the lreg `N bytes` field)
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921; mainline semantics verified in regs.h
evidence: party:R33-EE-GCC-3.2编译器行为手册与社区先例调研.md

laws.title: The EE register-pressure model is wider: struct allocno is 144 B and HARD_REG_SET is 192 bits

source_anchor.note: EE declaration line from DWARF; the mainline copy declares struct allocno at line 87. Field names and order match mainline.

symptom: a mainline-calibrated register-pressure model predicts the wrong spill count
lever: size the pressure model against 192 hard registers, not the mainline MIPS count
laws.receipt: DWARF byte_size 144; member step 24 B = 192 bits; disassembly stride 144 B (lea (%edi,%edi,8) then shl $0x4)
laws.falsifies: the assumption that mainline's HARD_REG_SET width applies to EE

laws.title: EE ships its own backend file config/mips/mips5900.c, which mainline 3.2.3 does not have

source_anchor.note: absent from mainline gcc-3.2.3 (config/mips/ checked); EE DWARF carries it as a compilation unit

symptom: a rule taken from mainline config/mips/mips.c does not reproduce EE code selection
lever: treat the EE backend as a separate source of rules; anchor it per symbol in mips5900.c
laws.receipt: cc1 embeds 135 source paths, including config/mips/mips5900.c; 152 functions resolve to that file; mainline 3.2.3 config/mips/ has no mips5900.c

laws.title: REG_FREQ is accumulated per register note, one block frequency per occurrence, and REG_FREQ_MAX is 1000

source_anchor.note: propagate_one_insn: REG_N_REFS += 1 and REG_FREQ += REG_FREQ_FROM_BB(bb) per register; also flow.c:3578 and flow.c:3413. regs.h:79 defines REG_FREQ_MAX 1000.

constants.means: the factor 10000 / REG_FREQ_MAX = 10, consumed by allocno_compare

symptom: a frequency proxy built from de-duplicated instructions lands adjacent pairs in the wrong order
a model built on de-duplicated instruction counts under-predicts the allocation order
lever: count every register occurrence, including a read-modify-write in one insn
laws.receipt: 75 functions / 1,004 adjacent pairs: counting every register occurrence reproduces the exact allocation order in 44/75 (mean Kendall tau 0.877) against 33/75 (0.873) for a de-duplicated instruction proxy — the source reading wins by 11 functions. The binary's 10.0 constant confirms the REG_FREQ_MAX = 1000 factor.
laws.falsifies: the reading that the factor is 1 (a misread of the global.c comment; recorded as P-108)
evidence: party:R33-EE-GCC-3.2编译器行为手册与社区先例调研.md

laws.title: Line numbers are not portable between trees: the EE snapshot drifts from mainline per function

source_anchor.note: measured against the EE binary: the same function is at global.c:789

binary_anchor.note: `find_reg` occurs twice in the shipped cc1: 0x08134570 (reload1.c:1685) and 0x081acd64 (global.c:1329). This law means the global.c one; always disambiguate by address, not by name.

symptom: a mainline line number is cited for an EE behaviour and the quoted lines do not contain that code
lever: cite the line number that addr2line reports for the shipped cc1, and keep the mainline line only as a cross-reference with its measured offset
laws.receipt: per-file median drift (EE line minus mainline line, gcc-3.2.3): global.c +341, gcse.c +137, haifa-sched.c +263, regmove.c +1920, reload1.c 0, local-alloc.c -4, cse.c -22, jump.c -47, loop.c -68, function.c -55, ifcvt.c -6; the same comparison against gcc-3.2.2 differs by at most 1 line, so the drift is EE's, not a point-release artefact
laws.falsifies: transplanting mainline line numbers into EE citations (the original R28 write-up quoted mainline line numbers only)

laws.title: There is no translation-unit level codegen state except the $L label counter

source_anchor.note: no source anchor yet; the rule comes from a controlled experiment

symptom: a one-TU-many-functions build is suspected of changing codegen
lever: merge or split translation units freely; only local label names shift, and they do not change the emitted bytes
laws.receipt: six TU configurations compared with normalised absolute addresses and jump-table deltas: instruction stream, .sdata and jump tables identical; only $L numbering shifts by one per preceding labelled function [R28 §4]
laws.falsifies: the fear that adding unrelated functions to a translation unit perturbs the target function
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2; the exact formula for the $L counter is still open

laws.title: In 23.greg, `regs to allocate` is the residue after local allocation, while `conflicts` lists every allocno

source_anchor.note: dump_conflicts: the count loop skips `reg_renumber >= 0` at line 1922 and prints at 1926; the conflicts loop at 1945 has no such test. The shipped binary resolves dump_conflicts to global.c:2265.

symptom: a value the dump reports was placed is treated as a hard register
a replay built from the conflict lines scores far below a simple heuristic
lever: take the still-unplaced allocnos from `regs to allocate` and the interference graph from `conflicts`
classify a conflict number as a hard register only when it is not an allocno (the allocno reg numbers are the `;; N conflicts:` keys and the `[N]` brackets in the RTL)
laws.receipt: 166 functions: the conflicts lines list 10,450 allocnos while `regs to allocate` lists 1,079 locally placed residue; the two differ in 166/166 functions (fx_arith: 8 vs 0). Misclassifying the extra numbers as hard registers was a measured failure mode in the colouring replay.
laws.falsifies: the reading that `conflicts` lists only the allocnos still waiting for a register
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 dumps; mainline semantics verified in global.c
evidence: party:R33-EE-GCC-3.2编译器行为手册与社区先例调研.md

laws.title: Delay slots are almost always filled with a real instruction; the leftover `nop` is the function-ending `jr ra`

source_anchor.note: dbr_schedule (mainline definition line; the shipped binary resolves it to reorg.c:3571, delta -11). The fillers are fill_simple_delay_slots and fill_slots_from_thread.

symptom: the target has a nop in a delay slot where the candidate has a real instruction
a basic block diffs by exactly one instruction
lever: treat a delay-slot difference as a scheduling decision, not an expression difference: regroup statements and check what the branch successors provide before editing the C
laws.receipt: 10 synthetic functions / 29 branches at -O2 -G0: 24 filled (82.8%), 0 nops emitted by the compiler, 5 branches followed by a label or the function end. Object-level check on f_dowhile: the `bgtz` slot holds `addiu`, the function-ending `jr ra` slot holds `nop`. Observed slot contents: addu 9, li 6, move 5, lw / sll / lui / ld 1 each.
laws.falsifies: the assumption that a nop delay slot means the scheduler found nothing to move; at this level the compiler emits none — the leftovers are filled by the assembler
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 -G0; 10 synthetic functions, no game code

laws.title: A switch becomes a jump table only when count >= 5 AND range <= 10 * count

source_anchor.note: expand_end_case_type branches to conditional branches when `count < case_values_threshold () || range > 10 * count || ...`; otherwise it calls try_tablejump (stmt.c:5509). expr.c:10486 defines CASE_VALUES_THRESHOLD as (HAVE_casesi ? 4 : 5). EE lines: expand_end_case_type stmt.c:5238, case_values_threshold expr.c:10431, try_tablejump expr.c:10595.

symptom: the target uses a jump table where the candidate uses a compare chain
a switch compiles to a table the candidate does not produce, or the reverse
lever: count the distinct cases and the (max - min) span before choosing a spelling: a table needs at least 5 cases and a span of at most 10 per case
moving case values closer together (or adding a range check before the switch) changes the decision
laws.receipt: 11 synthetic switches at -O2 -G0: dense 3 and 4 cases -> compare chain; dense 5, 6, 7, 8, 10, 16 -> table, table size exactly equal to the case count; cases {0,1,2,100,1000} (count 5, range 1000) -> chain; {0,10,20,30,40} (count 5, range 40 <= 50) -> table with 41 entries; {0,1,2,3,4,100,200,300} (count 8, range 300 > 80) -> chain. All 11 rows match the source rule. The table is emitted in section .rdata and referenced through a local label ($L9 in the synthetic fixture), jumped to with `jr $reg`; tools/compiler/ee-gcc-observe.py --selftest asserts this.
laws.falsifies: the external claim that five distinct cases are enough for a jump table (dds-decomp, ee-gcc 2.96, no licence): five cases are necessary but not sufficient, the span must also satisfy range <= 10 * count
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 -G0; 11 synthetic switches, no game code

laws.title: Float constants always come from the constant pool except 0.0f; a double is built inline when its low 32 bits are zero

source_anchor.note: The EE backend carries mips_move_1word, which mainline gcc-3.2.3 does not have; the exact constant-materialisation case lives in that file, which is not on this machine. The rule below is therefore measured, not read.

symptom: the target loads a constant from `.rodata` (l.s / l.d) where the candidate materialises it inline, or the reverse
a float constant diff that survives every source-level respelling
lever: a nonzero float constant always comes from the pool, so the residual is not the constant but the code around it
for a double, check the low 32 bits: zero means the value is built with dli + dsll inline, nonzero means the pool
laws.receipt: 14 float and 9 double constants at -O2 -G0. Floats: 0.0f -> `mtc1 $0`; 0.5f, 1.0f, 2.5f, 1.5f, -1.0f, 0.01f, 3.14f, 100.0f, -0.25f, 0.1f, 123.456f, 1e30f, 1e-30f, -0.0f -> all from the pool via %hi/%lo($LCn) + l.s, regardless of the low halfword. Doubles: 0.0 -> `move $2,$0`; 0.5, 1.0, 1.5, 2.5, 2^52 (low 32 bits zero) -> inline `dli`+`dsll`; 0.01, pi, 1.0000000001 (low 32 bits nonzero) -> pool via l.d.
laws.falsifies: the IDO 5.3 rule that the constant's low halfword decides inline versus pool for floats (n64-decomp-workbench L62, CC0): on ee-gcc 3.2 that split exists for doubles only
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 -G0; 23 synthetic constants, no game code. The binary anchor is a pointer into the EE backend, not a verification of the rule

laws.title: The frame is [vars][outgoing args][8 B per saved register]; the save area caps at 10 registers

source_anchor.note: find_reg decides which callee-saved register each allocno takes (EE binary: global.c:1329); the 8-byte slot and the 9-register $s budget come from the ABI, which mainline mips.h states and this backend inherits.

binary_anchor.note: `find_reg` occurs twice in the shipped cc1: 0x08134570 (reload1.c:1685) and 0x081acd64 (global.c:1329). This law means the global.c one; always disambiguate by address, not by name.

symptom: the candidate frame is larger than the target by a multiple of 8
you are about to reduce saved registers when the save area is already identical
lever: decompose the frame before editing: vars / outgoing args / 8 B per saved register
each saved register costs 8 B; beyond 10 saved registers more values can only spill into vars
laws.receipt: Synthetic dose-response (-O2 -G0, k values live across calls): k=2/4/6/8/10/12/14/18/24 -> frame 32/48/64/80/96/96/112/128/144 with regs= 4/6/8/10/10/10/10/10/10. The frame grows 8 B per saved register and the save area caps at 10 registers (80 B); beyond that only vars grows. The saved registers observed are $s0-$s7 (16-23), $fp (30) and $ra (31). Naming trap: the objdump in this toolchain prints register 30 as `s8` while the compiler's own assembly prints `$fp`, so counting names in a disassembly can mislead. Real function: func_001d4b88 retail frame 144 = vars 16 + args 48 + 10 saves (80); candidate frame 176 = vars 48 + args 48 + the same 10 saves, so the whole +32 B is the vars block. The cap is explained by the runtime register file read from a live cc1: the allocatable callee-saved GPRs are exactly {16..23, 30} (eight $s0-$s7 plus $fp), so with $ra the save area holds nine allocatable registers plus one return address = 10 slots. The dose-response was re-run on the other configuration this project uses - 3.2 at -O1 and 2.96 at -O2 - and the frame, regs and vars progression is identical row for row (k=2/4/6/8/10/12/16/20 -> frame 32/48/64/80/96/96/112/128, regs 4/6/8/10/10/10/10/10, vars 0/0/0/0/16/16/32/48).
laws.falsifies: the reading that a larger candidate frame means more saved registers, and the reading that the save area grows without bound with the number of live values
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 and -O1, and ee-gcc 2.96-ee-001003-1 at -O2; six to eight synthetic functions plus one real function. In the synthetic corpus a value that cannot take a register is sometimes rematerialised instead of spilled, so vars does not grow one slot per extra value.

laws.title: Signedness picks slt vs sltu; a type narrower than the register adds andi (unsigned) or sll+sra (signed); xori marks equality

source_anchor.note: No source anchor yet. The width/signedness extension is generic (mode versus word size) and the compare patterns live in the EE backend, which is not on this machine. Behaviour evidence only.

symptom: the candidate and the target differ by one instruction (`andi`, `sll` or `xori`) in front of the compare
a comparison against a constant produces a different instruction sequence after a type change
lever: read the extension instruction as the type's shape: `andi 0xff`/`0xffff` means an unsigned type narrower than the register; `sll`+`sra` means a signed narrow type; `slt`/`sltu` is the signedness
`xori $r,$r,C` followed by `sltu $r,$r,1` is an equality test, not a narrow-type marker
laws.receipt: 48 synthetic functions (8 types x 5 patterns x 2 contexts) at -O2 -G0. x < 100: int/ll -> slt; uint/ull -> sltu; signed char/short -> sll+sra, slt; unsigned char/short -> andi, sltu. x == 5: xori + sltu ...,1 for every type, with the same width prologue. x != 0: sltu (plus the width prologue). (x & 0x10) != 0: sra+andi for 32-bit types, andi+srl+andi for narrow types, dsrl+andi for 64-bit types.
laws.falsifies: the external claim that slt/sltiu versus xori distinguishes narrow unsigned types (dds-decomp, ee-gcc 2.96, no licence): xori marks equality, while narrowness shows up as an andi mask (unsigned) or an sll+sra extension (signed)
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 -G0; 48 synthetic functions, no game code

laws.title: Small-data addressing follows -G: objects up to the -G size go to .sdata/.sbss and are read as a bare symbol (gp_rel)

source_anchor.note: MIPS_DEFAULT_GVALUE is 8, so a build that passes no -G uses 8. The backend keeps mips_section_threshold (EE line config/mips/mips5900.c:226) and treats -1 as 'unset'; the shipped binary stores -1 there in the file and resolves it at startup.

constants.means: the 'unset' sentinel; the effective value comes from -G or MIPS_DEFAULT_GVALUE

symptom: the target reads a global as a bare symbol (`lw $2,g_int`) while the candidate emits lui %hi/%lo, or the reverse
an object lands in .sdata/.sbss in one build and .bss/.data in the other
lever: match the -G value to the target build before comparing globals: the project passes no -G, so the default 8 applies
objects up to 8 bytes (and not constants) become gp_rel; larger objects and every constant stay absolute
laws.receipt: One fixture with 4 B globals, an 8 B double, a 32 B array, a static const and a float constant, built at -G0/-G4/-G8/no flag: 4 B objects are absolute at -G0 and small-data at -G4/-G8/default; the 8 B double is absolute up to -G4 and small-data at -G8/default; the 32 B array is absolute everywhere; a static const read folds to an immediate; the float constant is absolute (%hi/%lo($LCn)) in every setting.
laws.falsifies: the implicit assumption that measurements taken at -G0 describe the project build: the project passes no -G, so its default is 8 and its small-data behaviour differs
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921; one fixture per setting. The build flags come from the project's MATCHED_CFLAGS (no -G).

laws.title: A value passed in the outgoing argument area is re-read from that slot after the call when it is an aggregate; a scalar gets a callee-saved register instead

source_anchor.note: store_one_arg (the shipped binary resolves it to calls.c:4284) writes the outgoing argument area; reusing that slot afterwards is the generic argument-store behaviour, not an EE addition. Promoting this to T1 needs the reuse logic read out of the shipped cc1's store_one_arg.

symptom: the frame grows by one 8 B slot for a value that is also passed to a call
the candidate spills an aggregate into the vars block while the target re-reads it from the outgoing argument area
lever: read the post-call use of an aggregate as a re-read of the outgoing slot: pass the same expression to the call and use it again afterwards
do not introduce a local copy of an aggregate that is passed to a call and used afterwards — the copy is a separate live object and costs a slot
laws.receipt: Two fixtures at -Os -G0 with more than eight parameters, so the ninth lands in the outgoing argument area. (A) a 4-byte struct is written to the outgoing slot, the call runs, and the post-call use re-reads the struct from that same slot (`lh $15,48($sp)`) with vars=0 and no extra frame. (B) a scalar is kept in a callee-saved register across the call (`addu $16,...` + `sd $16,64($sp)`), costing one 8 B save slot. A real function shows the same shape as (A): the retail target re-reads a 4-byte aggregate from its own outgoing slot after a recursive call.
laws.falsifies: the assumption that any value used after a call it was passed to must be spilled into the vars block or pinned in a callee-saved register
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -Os -G0; two synthetic fixtures plus one observation in a real function. Verified for a 4-byte aggregate and a scalar; other aggregate sizes are not measured.

laws.title: The EE register file is 140 hard registers in 29 classes: GPR 0-31, FP 32-63, HI/LO/HI1/LO1 64-67, FP_ACC 71, VU0 76-79 and 112-143, COP0 80-111

source_anchor.note: The class contents live in the EE backend's mips.h (REG_CLASS_CONTENTS), which is not on this machine; the line cited is the file that owns the EE register file. The values below are read from a live cc1, not from source.

symptom: you need to know whether a register is allocatable, caller-saved or reserved for this compiler
a replay or a diff assumes the mainline MIPS register file
lever: allocate only inside reg_class_contents[class] minus fixed_reg_set; for a call-crossing allocno also remove call_used_reg_set
the allocatable callee-saved GPRs are exactly {16..23, 30}: eight $s0-$s7 plus $fp, so with $ra the save area is 10 slots
laws.receipt: Read from a live cc1 (gdb, breakpoint at local_alloc, where init_reg_sets_1 has already filled the tables): 29 classes, ALL_REGS = 140 registers, HARD_REG_SET = 3 x 64 = 192 bits. GR_REGS = 0-31 (32), FP_REGS = 32-63 (32), HI/LO/HI1/LO1 = 64-67, ST = 68, ELIM = 69-70, FP_ACC = 71, 72-75 reserved, VU0_ACC = 76, VU0_Q/I/R = 77/78/79, COP0 = 80-111 (32), VU0 = 112-143 (32). fixed_reg_set leaves 0,1,26,27,28,29,31 fixed among the GPRs; call_used_reg_set leaves 2-15, 24, 25 caller-saved, so the allocatable callee-saved GPRs are {16..23, 30}.
laws.falsifies: the assumption that the shipped EE register file can be approximated by the mainline MIPS one, and the earlier guess that the runtime tables were unreadable (they are readable from a live process; only the static read returns zeros)
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921; read from a live cc1 on this machine. The class contents are compiler constants, not per-function decisions.

laws.title: The shipped global.c find_reg is not mainline's: a two-step alt_regs ladder whose decision is a side effect, not a return value

source_anchor.note: The shipped binary's DWARF puts find_reg's body at global.c:1336. The two-step ladder appears twice: global_alloc calls find_reg at global.c:400 (alt=0) and global.c:407 (alt=1), and global_init calls it at global.c:772 (alt=0) and global.c:777 (alt=1); find_reg also calls itself recursively at global.c:1540. Mainline gcc-3.2.3 declares the same name as find_reg (struct allocno *, HARD_REG_SET *), so this file's allocation core was reworked despite the shared name.

constants.means: the decision table the caller tests with cmpw/js

symptom: a port of mainline's allocation loop does not reproduce the recorded dispositions
an allocno is queried repeatedly with the same conflicts
lever: model the decision as a two-step ladder that writes the result as a side effect; alt_regs_p 0 is the first try and 1 the retry
do not read find_reg's return value: at the call sites it is discarded immediately
an allocno with no register is detected by the caller as a negative signed 16-bit entry, not by a return code
laws.receipt: gdb on the shipped cc1: `info args` at global.c:1336 prints find_reg (num=0, losers=0x0, alt_regs_p=0, accept_call_clobbered=0, retrying=0), where mainline declares find_reg (struct allocno *, HARD_REG_SET *). The function is called as a two-step ladder from two independent sites - 0x81aad68/0x81aadbe (global_init) and 0x81aa4ba/0x81aa520 (global_alloc) - with alt_regs_p 0 then 1 (losers NULL, the other flags zero in every observed call). At both external sites the return value is discarded: the instruction after the call immediately overwrites %eax (0x81aad6d, 0x81aa4bf), and the caller then reads a signed 16-bit per-register array (cmpw + js) to decide that an allocno has no register; one path also consults reg_alternate_class. So the choice is a side effect, not a return value, and the earlier reading of -1 in %eax was leftover. The same listing confirms sizeof(struct allocno) = 144 from the scaling (x9 then <<4) that indexes the allocno array. The call sites resolve to global.c:400/407 (global_alloc) and global.c:772/777 (global_init), and find_reg recurses at global.c:1540. The result lands in reg_renumber (a short array at 0x82ea1ec): the caller tests reg_renumber[pseudo] with cmpw + js.
laws.falsifies: the assumption that a replay built on mainline's find_reg can reproduce the shipped decisions (the structural reason a faithful replay scores 9.1%, and 9.9% with the real runtime class tables, against a 34.3% preference-first heuristic), and the reading that find_reg returns the chosen register
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921, observed on this machine with gdb; the retry ladder is shown for one fixture, other flag combinations (retrying, accept_call_clobbered) were zero in that sample

laws.title: Global allocation: preference first, then the lowest register left, after two passes that first avoid registers other allocnos prefer

source_anchor.note: The rule is the behaviour of the ladder at global.c:400/407 (see L-EE-017); it was fitted by measurement, not read from the shipped source.

symptom: you want to predict which hard register the compiler gives an allocno
a replay that bans every already-assigned register scores far below the naive heuristic
lever: pool = reg_class_contents[class] - fixed_reg_set, and for a call-crossing allocno also minus call_used_reg_set
ban only the allocno's hard_reg_conflicts plus the registers of the conflicting allocnos that are already placed
do NOT ban every already-assigned register: that double-counts what the conflict table already expresses
choose the first entry of the allocno's preference list that is still available, otherwise the lowest numbered candidate
the printed order is already the allocation order; do not re-sort it, and treat proxy sorts as noise
run two passes: the first also avoids the registers other allocnos prefer (regs_someone_prefers), the second drops that exclusion - this is what alt_regs_p toggles in the observed ladder
laws.receipt: On a 60/40 split of 75 functions (527 held-out allocnos with a recorded disposition): this rule reproduces 41.0% of the decisions, against 34.3% for the earlier preference-first heuristic and 9.1% for a replay modelled on mainline's find_reg two passes. Holding the dynamic conflict set at ground truth raises the same rule to 82.7%, so the residual is dominated by cascade from earlier wrong picks, not by the per-decision rule. Rule sweep over 888 allocnos: banning hard conflicts + dynamic conflicts 36.6%, adding the caller-saved exclusion for call-crossing allocnos 38.9%, banning all assigned registers 30.9%, and the two-pass 'someone prefers' variant 12.8%. Mismatch split: 160 the true register was banned, 368 the true register was a candidate but another was chosen, 15 the true register was outside the pool. Addressing detail verified live: allocno_order[i] holds an allocno index and allocno[index].reg holds the pseudo register number, so the dump's ';; N regs to allocate:' list prints the pseudos in allocation order; for the branchy fixture the live order [3,1,2,0,...] maps to the printed 152 150 151 149 ..., confirming that the printed list is the priority order. An attempt to substitute an external proxy order (n_refs descending 41.8%, live_length ascending 42.0%, against 38.9% for the printed order) is therefore a change of error pattern, not a better rule: the order is not the lever. Preference semantics measured exactly: of the 427 allocnos that carry a preference list, 323 pick the first entry that is still available and none picks a later entry, so 'first available preference' is the whole rule. A rotation start (scan from pseudo mod 32) lifts the corpus score to 49.1%, but it is a compensation artifact, not the scan order: with the dynamic conflict set held at ground truth the rotation scores 60.5% against 63.5% without it. Of the 334 no-preference mismatches, the true register was inside the computed candidate set in every case (none was banned), so the residual is the occupancy set, not the ban set or the scan order. A second pass structure was tested: adding 'avoid the registers that other allocnos prefer' (the EE-only regs_someone_prefers field) to the first pass raises the held-out score from 41.0% to 46.5% (corpus 38.9% -> 42.1%) while leaving the oracle-context score unchanged at 82.7%, i.e. it is a genuine rule rather than a compensation for the replay's own errors. (Contrast the rejected 'rotating start', which scores 60.5% against 63.5% under the oracle.) This matches both the EE-only struct field and the observed two-step ladder: alt_regs_p = 0 then 1. A final negative result closes the occupancy question: rebuilding the conflict set from the block-level live sets in the 16.life dump scores 30.6% against 42.1% for the dumped conflicts list, because block granularity merges allocnos that are live at different points, so the dumped list stays the better source. Two levers have therefore been tried and rejected (the rotating start, and live-range-derived occupancy); the remaining gap to the oracle ceiling is cascade, which needs instruction-level live ranges or the shipped source.
laws.falsifies: the two assumptions behind the earlier replays: that banning every already-assigned register is safe (it costs ~6 points), and that mainline's two-pass scan with a 'someone prefers' first pass is the shipped algorithm (12.8%); and the 'rotating start' reading (scan from pseudo mod 32) - it improves the end-to-end score by compensating for the replay's own errors, but it is worse than no rotation once the dynamic set is correct
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921, -O2/-Os corpus on this machine; the rule is measured for GPR allocnos and the readings come from a served-out split

laws.title: The float-constant rule is version-specific: 2.96 always materialises a float inline, 3.2 always loads non-zero floats from the pool

source_anchor.note: No source anchor: this is a measured difference between two shipped compilers. Full source for neither backend is available.

constants.means: the compiler this half of the law is measured on

symptom: a float constant loads from the pool in a 3.2 object but is materialised with lui/mtc1 in the same source compiled with 2.96
you applied L-EE-011 to CRI middleware code
lever: for 2.96 do not expect a constant pool for floats: expect lui (plus ori when the low 16 bits of the bit pattern are non-zero) followed by mtc1
for 3.2 expect lui/addiu/lwc1 from the pool for every non-zero float (L-EE-011)
laws.receipt: Same fixtures, both compilers, flags -O2 -G0, reading the OBJECT code (2.96 writes li.s in the assembly, which is misleading). 3.2: every non-zero float is lui + addiu + lwc1 from the pool; 0.0f is mtc1 from the zero register. 2.96: every float is materialised inline - lui + mtc1 when the low 16 bits of the pattern are zero (0.5f, 1.0f, 2.5f, -1.0f, 100.0f), lui + ori + mtc1 when they are not (0.01f, 3.14f, 123.456f, 1e30f), and plain mtc1 for 0.0f. Doubles agree between the two compilers: move for 0.0, li + dsll32 when the low 32 bits are zero, pool (lui + ld) otherwise. The narrow-compare idioms (L-EE-013), the switch threshold (L-EE-010) and -G0 absolute addressing (L-EE-014) were also re-run on 2.96 and agree.
laws.falsifies: the assumption that the float rule of L-EE-011 transfers to the other compiler this project uses (2.96 builds the CRI middleware)
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 and ee-gcc 2.96-ee-001003-1 at -O2 -G0, synthetic fixtures only; the object code was read with the MIPS objdump

laws.title: The pass pipeline is -O sensitive: -O1 runs 20 of the 26 dumps and skips sibling-call, gcse, regmove, both schedulers and range; -O0 runs 9

source_anchor.note: The pipeline is driven from toplev.c (the same file that calls global_alloc at line 3316). The pass set per level is measured with -da rather than read from the shipped source.

symptom: a function only matches at -O1 and you are looking for a source-level difference
a pass dump you expected is missing
lever: check the -O level before comparing code shape: at -O1 there is no 19.regmove, 20.sched, 21.range, 29.sched2, 11.gcse or 01.sibling, so expect scheduling and instruction-order differences
count the -da dumps only for a compile that succeeded: a rejected source leaves a partial set
laws.receipt: `ee-gcc -<level> -G0 -da -c` on one loop fixture yields 9 dumps at -O0, 20 at -O1, 26 at -O2 and 26 at -Os. The six missing at -O1 are 01.sibling, 11.gcse, 19.regmove, 20.sched, 21.range and 29.sched2. The decision rules themselves do not change: at -O1 a 0.5f constant still loads from the pool, a low-word-zero double is still built with li + dsll32, and a dense six-case switch still becomes a table - only the instruction order and the register moves differ. A source that fails to compile (for example a C99 for-loop declaration under C89) leaves just two dumps, so a dump count is only meaningful for a successful compile.
laws.falsifies: the assumption that one pass inventory describes the compiler: at -O1 six passes do not run, which is why some project functions match only at that level
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O0/-O1/-O2/-Os on this machine; the inventory was counted on one loop fixture and the rule checks on four synthetic fixtures

laws.title: gp_rel needs a definition in this translation unit placed in .sdata/.sbss; 'weak' does not help, and an extern reference stays absolute at every -G

source_anchor.note: Which objects count as small data is decided in the backend plus varasm.c; no line could be read from the shipped tree, so the rule is measured. See L-EE-014 for the -G threshold itself.

constants.means: the 'unset' sentinel; -G or the default 8 decides the threshold

symptom: a global is addressed with lui %hi/%lo where the target uses the bare symbol, or the reverse
you declared an object with a small-data section attribute but the addressing did not change
lever: at -G0 the only way to get gp_rel is to define the object in this translation unit with section(".sdata") or section(".sbss")
weak is irrelevant to the choice: a weak object without a section attribute stays absolute
an extern declaration cannot be made small-data in any -G setting - the definition has to be in the same translation unit
laws.receipt: Assembly-level test at -O2 with -G0, the default (-G8) and -G8. Definitions in this unit: a plain int and a weak int are addressed with lui %hi at -G0 and as a bare symbol at the default; the same objects with section(".sbss") or section(".sdata") are addressed as a bare symbol at -G0 as well, with or without weak. Extern-only references (no definition in the unit) are addressed with lui %hi in every setting, even when the declaration carries a section attribute. objdump -t confirms the section attribute wins for placement: section(".sbss") lands in .sbss and section(".sdata") in .sdata, while a weak object without an attribute lands in .bss.
laws.falsifies: the reading that a weak small-data definition is what produces gp_rel: the section attribute is the operative part, and an extern declaration cannot produce it at all
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 with -G0/-G8/default, synthetic declarations; a link is not needed to observe the addressing form

laws.title: Functions are 8-byte aligned by default; -falign-functions=4 removes the padding between small functions, and -ffunction-sections alone does not

source_anchor.note: Function alignment comes from the assembler directives the backend emits (ASM_OUTPUT_ALIGN); no line was read from the shipped tree, so the rule is measured.

constants.means: the default function alignment in bytes

symptom: objdiff reports a size or offset mismatch while the instructions themselves agree
function symbols sit 16 bytes apart when the function is 12 bytes long
lever: the default function alignment is 8 bytes, so a 12-byte function is padded to 16; -falign-functions=4 aligns to 4 and packs them tightly
-ffunction-sections puts each function in its own .text.N section but does NOT remove the 8-byte alignment unless -falign-functions=4 is also given
the project builds with -O2 -falign-functions=4 -ffunction-sections, so expect each function section to be exactly the function size, 4-byte aligned
laws.receipt: Four 12-byte functions in one unit at -O2 -G0. No alignment flag: the assembly carries .align 2 plus .p2align 3,,7, the symbols sit at 0x0/0x10/0x20/0x30 and .text is 0x40 bytes - 4 bytes of padding per function. With -falign-functions=4 the .p2align disappears, the symbols sit at 0x0/0xc/0x18/0x24 and .text is 0x30 - no padding. -falign-functions=8 reproduces the default. With -ffunction-sections each function lands in .text.N of 0x10 bytes, still carrying .p2align 3 inside; only the combination -falign-functions=4 -ffunction-sections yields 0x0c-byte sections, i.e. sections exactly the size of the function.
laws.falsifies: the assumption that -ffunction-sections alone removes inter-function padding, and the assumption that function alignment is 4 bytes by default
laws.scope: ee-gcc 3.2-ee-040921 at -O2 -G0 on this machine; four synthetic one-instruction functions, so the padding effect is at its most visible
